'''Robert Anthony Kowalski''' (born 15 May 1941) is an American-British [[logician]] and [[computer scientist]], whose research is concerned with developing both human-oriented models of computing and computational models of human thinking.<ref name="archivesit">{{cite web| url=https://archivesit.org.uk/interviews/robert-bob-kowalski/ | title=Interview with Robert (Bob) Kowalski | work=Archives IT | accessdate=3 August 2023 }}</ref> He has spent most of his career in the United Kingdom.

==Education==
He was educated at the [[University of Chicago]], [[University of Bridgeport]] (BA in mathematics, 1963), [[Stanford University]] (MSc in mathematics, 1966), [[University of Warsaw]] and the [[University of Edinburgh]] (PhD in [[computer science]], 1970).<ref name="archivesit" />

==Career==
He was a [[research fellow]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]] (1970–75) and has been at the [[Department of Computing, Imperial College London]] since 1975, attaining a chair in [[computational logic]] in 1982 and becoming emeritus professor in 1999.<ref name="archivesit" />

He began his research in the field of [[automated theorem proving]], developing both [[SLD resolution|SL-resolution]]<ref>Kowalski, R. and Kuehner, D., "Linear Resolution with Selection Function", in [[Artificial Intelligence (journal)|Artificial Intelligence]], Vol. 2, 1971, pp. 227–260. Reprinted in ''Anthology of Automated Theorem-Proving Papers'', Vol. 2, [[Springer-Verlag]], 1983, pp. 542–577.</ref> with Donald Kuehner and the connection graph proof procedure.<ref>Kowalski, R., "A Proof Procedure Using Connection Graphs", in ''[[Journal of the ACM]]'' Vol. 22, No. 4, 1975, pp. 572–595.</ref> He developed [[SLD resolution]] and the procedural interpretation of [[Horn clauses]],<ref>Kowalski, R., "Predicate Logic as Programming Language", in Proceedings IFIP Congress, Stockholm, [[North-Holland Publishing Company|North-Holland Publishing Co.]], 1974, pp. 569–574. Reprinted in Computers for Artificial Intelligence Applications, (eds. Wah, B. and Li, G.-J.), [[IEEE Computer Society Press]], Los Angeles, 1986, pp. 68–73.</ref> which underpin the operational semantics of [[backward reasoning]] in [[logic programming]]. With [[Maarten van Emden]],<ref>van Emden, M. and Kowalski, R., "The Semantics of Predicate Logic as a Programming Language", in ''Journal of the ACM'', Vol. 23, No. 4, 1976, pp. 733–742.</ref> he also developed the minimal model and the fixpoint semantics of Horn clauses, which underpin the logical semantics of logic programming.

With Marek Sergot, he developed both the [[event calculus]]<ref>Kowalski, R. and Sergot, M., "A Logic-based Calculus of Events", in ''New Generation Computing'', Vol. 4, No. 1, February 1986, pp. 67–95. Also in ''Knowledge Base Management-Systems'', (eds. C. Thanos and J. W. Schmidt), Springer-Verlag, pp. 23–51. Also in The Language of Time: A Reader (eds. Inderjeet Mani, J. Pustejovsky, and R. Gaizauskas). [[Oxford University Press]], 2005.</ref> and the application of logic programming to [[Applications of artificial intelligence to legal informatics|legal reasoning]].<ref>Sergot, M., Sadri, F., Kowalski, R., Kriwaczek, F., Hammond, P., and Cory, T., "The British Nationality Act as a Logic Program", in ''[[Communications of the ACM]]'', Vol. 29, No. 5, 1986, pp. 370–386.</ref><ref name="Kowalski, R. 1992, pp. 203">Kowalski, R., "Legislation as Logic Programs", in Logic Programming in Action (eds. G. Comyn, N. E. Fuchs, M. J. Ratcliffe), Springer-Verlag, 1992, pp. 203–230.</ref> Together, Kowalski and Sergot supervised one of the first use cases of a [[legal expert system]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eliot |first=Lance |date=2021-04-17 |title=AI & Law: British Nationality Act Unexpectedly Spurred AI And Law |url=https://lance-eliot.medium.com/ai-law-british-nationality-act-unexpectedly-spurred-ai-and-law-404aea03386a |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=Medium |language=en}}</ref> With Fariba Sadri, he developed an agent model<ref>Kowalski, R., "Using Metalogic to Reconcile Reactive with Rational Agents". In ''Meta-Logics and Logic Programming'' (K. Apt and F. Turini, eds.), [[MIT Press]], 1995.</ref><ref>Kowalski, R. and Sadri, F., "From Logic Programming towards Multi-agent Systems", ''Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence'', Volume 25 (1999), pp. 391–419.</ref> in which beliefs are represented by logic programs and goals are represented by [[integrity constraints]].

Kowalski was one of the developers of [[abductive logic programming]], in which logic programs are augmented with integrity constraints and with undefined, abducible predicates.<ref>Eshghi, K., and Kowalski, R., "Abduction through deduction". [[Department of Computing, Imperial College London|Department of Computing]], [[Imperial College London|Imperial College]], 1988.</ref><ref>Kakas, T., Kowalski, K. and Toni, F., "Abductive Logic Programming". ''[[Journal of Logic and Computation]]'', 1992, Vol. 2 No. 6, pp. 719–770.</ref> This work led to the demonstration with Phan Minh Dung and [[Francesca Toni]] that most logics for default reasoning can be regarded as special cases of assumption-based [[argumentation]].<ref>Bondarenko, A., Dung, P. M., Kowalski, R., and Toni, F. " An Abstract Argumentation-theoretic Approach to Default Reasoning". ''[[Journal of Artificial Intelligence]]'', 93(1–2), 1997, pp 63–101.</ref><ref>Dung, P. M., Kowalski, R., and Toni, F. "Dialectic proof procedures for assumption-based, admissible argumentation". ''Journal of Artificial Intelligence'', 170(2), February 2006, pp. 114–159.</ref>

In his 1979 book, ''Logic for Problem Solving'',<ref>Kowalski, R.A., 1979. [http://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~rak/papers/LogicForProblemSolving.pdf] Logic for Problem Solving, Elsevier, North Holland.</ref> Kowalski argues that logical inference provides a simple and powerful model of problem solving that can be used by both humans and computers. In his 2011 book, ''Computational Logic and Human Thinking – How to be Artificially Intelligent'',<ref>Kowalski, R.A., 2011. [http://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~rak/papers/newbook.pdf] Computational Logic and Human Thinking – How to be Artificially Intelligent, Cambridge University Press.</ref> he argues that the use of [[computational logic]] can help ordinary people to improve their natural language communication skills, and that in combination with [[decision theory]], it can be used to improve their practical problem-solving abilities.

In joint work with Fariba Sadri, he developed the logic and computer language Logic Production Systems (LPS),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lps.doc.ic.ac.uk |title = LPS {{!}} Logic Production Systems | publisher=[[Imperial College London]] | location=UK }}</ref><ref>Kowalski, R., Sadri, F., Calejo, M. and Dávila, J., 2023. "Combining logic programming and imperative programming in LPS". Prolog: The Next 50 Years (pp. 210-223). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.</ref> which integrates much of his previous work on computational logic.

More recently, he has been developing Logical English (LE) as syntactic sugar for Prolog and other logic programming languages. Although writing LE requires special training, understanding LE requires only a reading knowledge of English. Kowalski argues that the restricted syntax of LE resembles the syntax of well-written legal rules and regulations,<ref name="Kowalski, R. 1992, pp. 203"/> and he has helped to develop several applications of LE for redrafting legal contracts.<ref>Kowalski, R. and Datoo, A., 2021. Logical English Meets Legal English for Swaps and Derivatives. Artificial Intelligence and Law, Online 12 August 2021, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10506-021-09295-3.</ref><ref>John Cummins, Jacinto Davila, Robert Kowalski, David Ovenden. 2024. Computable Contracts for Insurance – Establishing an Insurance-Specific Controlled Natural Language InsurLE.. In The British Insurance Law Association Journal, Issue Number: 136</ref> He has also advocated its use for introducing logical thinking and writing in education.<ref>Kowalski, R., Dávila, J., Sartor, G. and Calejo, M., 2023. "Logical English for law and education". Prolog: The Next 50 Years (pp. 287-299). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.</ref>

Kowalski has a long history of involvement with the use of logic programming to help teach logic at all educational levels, starting with a course of lessons in 1978 for 12-year-old children at his daughters' middle school.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~rak/history.pdf |title = A Short Story of My Life and Work April 2002 - revised June 2015 | publisher=[[Imperial College London]] | location=UK }}</ref><ref>Kowalski, R., "Logic as a Computer Language for Children", in Proceedings of European Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Orsay, France, July 1982. Reprinted in New Horizons in Educational Computing, (ed. M. Yazdani), Ellis Horwood Ltd., Chichester, 1984, pp. 121-144. Reprinted in Progress in Artificial Intelligence, (eds. L. Steel and J. A. Campbell), Ellis Horwood Ltd., Chichester.</ref> These early lessons used a child-friendly syntax for Prolog, which contributed to the later development of Logical English. He is continuing to contribute to the mission of teaching logical thinking through logic programming as co-chair of the Prolog Education Group.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://prolog-lang.org/Education/ |title=Prolog Education}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
Kowalski was elected a Fellow of the [[Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence|American Association for Artificial Intelligence]] in 1991, of the European Co-ordinating Committee for Artificial Intelligence in 1999, and of the [[Association for Computing Machinery]] in 2001.<ref name="archivesit" />

In 2011, he received the [[IJCAI Award for Research Excellence]] for his contributions to logic in [[knowledge representation]] and problem solving, including work on automated theorem proving and logic programming.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cs.nmsu.edu/ALP/2012/01/book-review-computational-logic-and-human-thinking-how-to-be-artificially-intelligent/|title=Book review: Computational Logic and Human Thinking: How to be Artificially Intelligent – Association for Logic Programming|access-date=1 May 2022|archive-date=28 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221228150806/https://www.cs.nmsu.edu/ALP/2012/01/book-review-computational-logic-and-human-thinking-how-to-be-artificially-intelligent/|url-status=dead}}</ref> He received a [[Japan Society for the Promotion of Science]] Award for Eminent Scientists for 2012–2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jsps.go.jp/english/e-awards/list.html|title=JSPS awards for eminent scientists|website=jsps.go.jp|access-date=24 June 2018|archive-date=8 February 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220208151815/https://www.jsps.go.jp/english/e-awards/list.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2021, Kowalski, Fariba Sadri and Marek Sergot received the inaugural CodeX Prize for their application of logic programming to the formalisation and analysis of the [[British Nationality Act 1981|British Nationality Act]]. Their 1986 paper, "The British Nationality Act as a Logic Program", published in ''[[Communications of the ACM]]'', was recognised as a pioneering work in computational law.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://law.stanford.edu/press/new-codex-prize-awarded-to-computational-law-pioneers-during-9th-annual-codex-futurelaw-conference/ | title=New CodeX Prize Awarded to Computational Law Pioneers During 9th Annual CodeX FutureLaw Conference|publisher=Stanford Law School|date= 8 April 2021}}</ref>
